sources.news_title: Brazil election 'tsunami' sends currency and stock market tumbling
Lula mobilized millions to win Brazil's election, while Bolsonaro contests victory
sources.text:
BRAZIL – President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential runoff Sunday is facing its first hurdle as his competitor, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, attempts to mount an organized opposition to the results.
Lula, who convinced an extra 10.4 million voters to support him in the runoff, is expected to take office on Jan. 5, 2027, for his fourth non-consecutive term. He will serve as a counterweight in a region where leaders are shifting to the right and aligning with U.S. President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, promised to cozy up to the Trump administration.
Recommended Videos
President Donald Trump suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Lula’s reelection was “rigged.”
“Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me,” Trump told reporters before flying to Mississippi for a rally. He added, “I thought it had a very bad look, the way it was tabulated.”
Trump also said: “It looked like another rigged election, frankly.”
At a news conference Sunday, Bolsonaro said he planned to request an annulment of the election following a chaotic extension of voting at the request of both candidates. But in a video on his social media channels on Monday he did not repeat that message and promised to organize opposition to Lula.
Bolsonaro said he will press the electoral court to nullify the election results, which it has never done before.
That would be a high hurdle: Bolsonaro would have to present evidence that the 4.4 million votes by which Lula won the election were fraudulent — and convince the full eight-member electoral court of that. He would need to do that before the election results are certified on Dec.18.
“I am going to gather elected lawmakers and senators to organize our strategy and make the lower house and the Senate our fortress against barbaric acts that are set to happen in another four years of Lula,” Bolsonaro said.
Bolsonaro also said he visited his father in house arrest on Monday. Jair Bolsonaro, who is now serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt, unsuccessfully contested his loss to Lula four years ago.
Early signs from Brazil’s institutions and from leaders across the region, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the results will be respected nationally and internationally.
Even with the vote extension, Lula’s win was decisive. The soon-to-be 81-year-old incumbent won more than 64 million votes compared to just under 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.
President of Brazil’s electoral authority, Kassio Nunes, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, was among those who recognized Lula’s victory Sunday.
“This is a really uphill battle for Flavio Bolsonaro. Important Brazilian power brokers are closing ranks behind Lula, sometimes begrudgingly," said Brian Winter, Brazil analyst and editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly.
“I sense that Brazilian power brokers that matter don’t really want to go down the path of a truly contested election,” he said.
The numbers behind Lula's victory
The key to Lula’s win was the additional 14.1 million voters who showed up for the second-round election, including those who voted for other candidates in the first round. Analysts say three-quarters of those votes went to Lula, handing him the victory. And notably, the first round set a record for the number of Brazilians who decided not to vote, while the second round had the least number of abstentions ever.
Lula gave his digital campaign to lawmaker André Janones, who mounted a fierce and persistent social media operation that mobilized many of those previously uncommitted voters. Janones' key tool was a channel on messaging app WhatsApp called “Lula's Army,” which gathered almost 11 million people and mobilized them to campaign via social media for the incumbent.
Janones “basically embraced the right’s style of aggressive politics, very intense, constant messaging,” said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of International Relations at Fundação Getulio Vargas in Sao Paulo.
“The defeat in the first round jolted the Lula campaign into action. The strategy during the first round was lackluster and saw a lot of infighting,” Stuenkel said.
Juliano Cortinhas, international relations professor at the University of Brasília, said Lula's social media initiative in the runoff was also key to pressuring Meta, the owner of Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook, to end what the president's campaign denounced as bias helping Bolsonaro.
Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on Oct.15 that Meta must adopt measures that assure equal treatment of the two presidential candidates, which the company later said it addressed.
There was “external interference we were suffering by major platforms,” Cortinhas said. “It wasn't only Meta, many others were using their algorithms to repost many images and many messages of the far-right, and they did not do the same to the left.”
It was the first time since 1989 that a candidate came from behind in the first round to win in the second.
Results show voter turnout surged overall, particularly in wealthier metropolitan centers, but Lula achieved his highest gains in lower-income municipalities where his base was already established. He mobilized former non-voters, those who voted blank in the first round and supporters of third-party candidates.
Jorge Henrique Oliveira Sena, a 26-year-old maintenance worker in Brasilia, was one of those who didn’t vote in the first round. Neither candidate excited him much, but he cast his vote for Lula. “It’s not a question of supporting, but between the two, I had more of a connection with him,” he said.
Brazil's voting system and Sunday's disruptions
Brazil holds general elections every four years, and its electronic voting machines have made the tallying process quick and secure.
Brazilian authorities adopted electronic voting machines in the 1990s to combat fraud and the system has been largely reliable since then. Results are usually reported mere hours after polls close.
In the lead-up to the 2022 vote, Jair Bolsonaro repeatedly cast unfounded doubts on Brazil’s electronic voting system. No significant fraud has ever been detected.
But the usually swift voting process was thrown into disarray Sunday after a last-minute decision to extend voting nationwide at both candidates’ requests.
Lula made the request because of issues with public transportation in metropolis, Sao Paulo, and the northeastern city of Salvador, two of his strongholds. Bolsonaro requested it after heavy rains in the south, which he won by a strong margin in the first round.
The decision was made by a Supreme Court justice mere minutes before polls were set to close at 5 p.m. and the speed of Brazil’s counting process meant many polling stations didn’t receive the news until they were already wrapping up.
Yet given the reliability of Brazil's voting system and Lula's win by a significant margin, a path to annul the results could be difficult for Bolsonaro.
Benjamin Gedan, senior fellow and director of the Stimson Center Latin America program, said Bolsonaro's rejection of his loss was not surprising.
“False claims of fraud are becoming commonplace, though that does not make them any less dangerous," he said. He noted “Lula’s margin of victory, and the quick recognition of the result by conservative leaders in the region."
Nevertheless, Lula still faces challenges moving forward, including political polarization in the country, a possible fiscal crisis and a right-wing Congress in which Bolsonaro's party will have more seats than any other. Bolsonaro himself remains a senator, though his term ends in January.
“We shouldn’t underestimate the power of the Bolsonaro family," said Winter, the Brazil analyst. "They can make life difficult for Lula for weeks and months to come.”
___
Savarese reported from Sao Paulo. AP writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed.

To recap: Brazilian polling stations are supposed to close at 5 p.m. sharp. A last-minute extension from a Supreme Court justice - who once happened to be the president's personal attorney - extended voting for two additional hours. This word arrived too late for many areas considered Bolsonaro strongholds. Their election officials were caught by surprise, had closed the polls and shut down the machines as prescribed, and sealed the boxes holding the ballots.
There were no do-overs or restarts possible.
Strangely enough, as Lula-friendly districts seemed to be lagging in closing up shop to begin with, they weren't bothered by the short notice on the extended hours and kept the doors open for all comers. Unsurprisingly, Lula votes soared.

All four lawyers interviewed call the situation unprecedented. “This is an extremely serious, critical situation,” said Priscilla Sodré Pereira, an electoral lawyer. Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin decided, minutes before polls closed, to extend all polling stations by two additional hours. By the time of the announcement, some polling centers had already closed, their voting machines had shut down, and they could not reopen. Fernnado Neisser, an electoral law professor at Fundação Getulio Vargas, a Brazilian research institute, said the election could be annulled if the margin is very narrow and it is shown that polling stations stayed open longer in areas that strongly favor one candidate.

sources.news_title: Lula secures historic fourth term as Ramaphosa hails 'victory for the Global South'
sources.text:
The leftist Lula pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday, clinching a re-election victory, but his rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, refused to accept the loss.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has hailed Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s historic fourth-term election victory as a win for the Global South, reaffirming South Africa’s commitment to strengthening ties with its key Brics partner.
The leftist Lula pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday, clinching a re-election victory, but his rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, refused to accept the loss and said he would seek to annul the vote.
Conservative wave
With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries, such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.
Da Silva, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term.
According to official results, he won 51.8 percent of the votes to 48.2 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, with Lula pulling around 4.4 million more votes.
Ramaphosa said Brazil and South Africa maintain a close bilateral and strategic relationship founded on South-South cooperation, multilateralism and shared leadership within BRICS, IBSA, the G77+China, and the G20.
Ramaphosa
In March 2026, Ramaphosa undertook a state visit to Brazil at Lula’s invitation, with the Presidency explaining that the visit further strengthened the existing bilateral trade and political relationship.
“On behalf of the government and the people of South Africa, I congratulate my dear brother and friend, President Lula and the people of Brazil. This victory will echo beyond the shores of Brazil. It is a victory for the Global South and progressive forces throughout the world,” Ramaphosa said.
“We affirm our commitment to continue strengthening bilateral relations between our two countries and working closely together in all multilateral fora to forge a just and better world order underpinned by solidarity and adherence to international law.”
Brazil voting
Sunday’s vote was mired in confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, even as some polling stations had already closed, according to AFP.
The move came at Lula’s request, who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.
Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.
Lula’s triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America’s largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Trump’s demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs.

“This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed,” he said. He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil’s sovereignty.
“Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil,” he said. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard.”
In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro’s signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

He then helped found the Workers’ Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014 but impeached two years later.

He was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil’s Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of Jair Bolsonaro’s biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.
Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration, and boosted several government initiatives.

sources.text:
Lula Wins Record Fourth Term in Brazil Presidential Elections
Lula's victory marks a setback for the Bolsonaro family's hopes of returning to the presidency following the conviction of former President Jair Bolsonaro over an attempted coup
Left leader, 80-year-old former factory worker and current Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won re-election on Sunday, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a heated runoff after the two candidates were closely matched in the first round of voting.
According to Brazilian media and projections by Datafolha, with 99.77 per cent of the votes counted, the incumbent president secured 51.76 per cent of the valid votes in the second round, compared to 48.24 per cent for Bolsonaro.
The victory allows the Workers' Party leader to extend his record as one of Brazil's longest-serving presidents, behind Getúlio Vargas. By the end of his latest term, Lula will have spent 16 years in power, marking a record in Brazil's democratic history.
The victory follows a campaign dominated by concerns over the cost of living, crime and corruption. CNN reported that this was also the first time since the return of direct presidential elections in 1989 that a candidate had won the presidency after finishing second in the first round.
Lula, who first governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010, faced a challenging re-election battle amid concerns over living costs and public security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to reduce food prices.
Both presidential candidates faced corruption allegations involving family members and associates. Lula had spent more than a year in prison following corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.
The results of Sunday's runoff came after a heated election day, with voting extended by two hours following last-minute appeals from both candidates to electoral authorities.
According to CNN, Lula's victory is expected to have implications beyond Brazil, keeping Latin America's largest country on a more independent foreign-policy path. Lula has emphasised Brazil's sovereignty and closer ties with the Global South and China amid tensions with the Trump administration.
Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He later helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times before winning the election in 2002.
He was re-elected in 2006 and was succeeded by his cabinet minister Dilma Rousseff in 2010. Rousseff won re-election in 2014.

sources.news_title: Conservative wave hits roadblock in Brazil as Lula holds off Bolsonaro challenge
sources.text:
Incumbent leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated conservative Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential runoff, according to The Associated Press. The deeply polarized nation returned to the polls for a second round runoff on Sunday.
Bolsonaro narrowly won the first round on Oct. 4, with 47% of the vote, to Lula's 45%, but fell short of the 50% majority required to win the election outright.
BRAZIL BECOMES NEXT TEST FOR LATIN AMERICA’S SURGING CONSERVATIVE MOVEMENT
The victory marks an unprecedented fourth presidential term for Lula, and a remarkable comeback victory. The result is even more surprising given that Bolsonaro had led, albeit by tight margins, in recent polling, and Brazil had recently elected a conservative congress aligned with the Bolsonaro agenda.
Earlier in the day, Lula voted in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Sao Paulo, while Bolsonaro voted in the north of Rio de Janeiro, the state he represents in the Senate.
The first vote tallies came in from Brazilians living overseas, where Lula won a decisive victory in Germany, and Bolsonaro won an overwhelming victory in Japan.
BRAZIL’S RAPID ELECTION COUNT PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON VOTING SECURITY AHEAD OF US MIDTERMS
While Bolsonaro performed well in his southern electoral strongholds, winning by comfortable margins in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná, and Rio Grande do Sul, he won those states by smaller margins than in the first round.
His turnout in the south was not enough to overcome Lula's famed Northeastern firewall; a reflection of the Workers Party dominance in the country's populous "Nordeste" region.
Bolsonaro also turned in a disappointing performance in Minas Gerais, which geographically and politically straddles the Brazilian north/south divide. Often referred to as the nation's quintessential bellwether state, it is fair to say that as goes Minas Gerais, so goes the nation.
While Bolsonaro won Minas Gerais by 5% in the first round, in the second round it was essentially tied.
Bolsonaro had received endorsements from other first round candidates: best-selling author Augusto Cury, former Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema, and former Goiás Governor Ronaldo Caiado.
LATIN AMERICA’S CONSERVATIVE SHIFT FACES ITS BIGGEST TEST YET IN BRAZIL ELECTION
However, they were not enough to overcome the much-respected electoral machinery of the Workers Party. Lula has now appeared on the presidential ballot 7 times, winning 4 of those elections.
Heading into the first round, Flavio Bolsonaro was effectively able to make the case to working-class and middle-class voters that the Lula's economic approach was driving up their cost of living.
He painted the Lula administration as bloated, tax-heavy, and given to racking up debt and tied this to inflation and kitchen table economics.
Additionally, his message of hardline law and order appealed to a Brazilian public where voters routinely suggest that violence is the most pressing issue.
Nonetheless, these economic and security concerns were not enough to overcome a generation of loyalty to the Workers Party and its social programs, particularly in the North and Northeast of the country, where Lula won by wide margins.
While Lula will be riding high heading into a historic fourth term in office, he will face a Congress with a center-right and right-wing majority that has been described as one of the most conservative in history.
While Flavio Bolsonaro lost the 2026 election by a narrow margin, the Bolsonaro movement is certainly not going away, and arguably remains an influential force in modern Brazilian politics.
The Lula victory also brings to an end a long string of victories for Trump-backed right-wing candidates across the region. While Trump had not officially endorsed Flavio Bolsonaro, he made no secret of his preference, and enjoyed a close relationship with the Bolsonaro family.
Looking forward to 2030, all eyes will turn to Bolsonaro clan ally Tarcisio de Freitas, who stepped aside this election cycle, in order to clear the way for Flavio Bolsonaro's run. Will the Brazilian right back another Bolsonaro in four years time, or will the popular São Paulo governor also mount a bid?
In addition to the presidential election, voters in five states, as well as the federal district of Brasília, were also selecting governors in runoff elections. Bolsonaro-aligned candidates appeared poised to win most of those races.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

In brief
- Brazil’s stock market lost more than $200 billion in value at Monday’s open, and the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) fell as much as 26% after Lula beat Flávio Bolsonaro.

Brazil’s stock market lost more than $200 billion in value at the open on Monday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff, a result that prediction markets had priced at roughly a one in five chance.
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, ticker EWZ, a basket of Brazilian stocks that trades in New York like a single share, fell as much as 26% from Friday’s close of about $42.60, touching $31.40 before trimming the loss to about 23% at $32.84 by 10:38 a.m. ET.
That is memecoin-sized volatility for a fund built around Brazil’s biggest companies, and it leaves EWZ roughly where it started 2026 after a 34% gain through Friday.
The dollar rose as much as 12% against the real on Friday, while the Ibovespa, Brazil’s benchmark stock index, fell as much as 17% to about 170,000 points. For a dollar-based investor, those moves at their worst combine to a loss of about 26%, in line with the ETF’s low.
B3, the São Paulo exchange, halted trading for 30 minutes after the Ibovespa fell 10% from Friday’s close, its first circuit breaker since the COVID-19 pandemic. A circuit breaker is an automatic pause meant to slow panic selling, but the index kept sliding after trading resumed.
Investors had been positioning for the opposite result since Bolsonaro unexpectedly finished first in the Oct. 4 first round, with 47.03% of valid votes to Lula’s 45.16%. The Ibovespa jumped 7.85% the next day and EWZ gained more than 10% on bets that Bolsonaro would tighten public finances and open the way to lower interest rates. Monday’s drop erased that rally and, at its lows, left the Ibovespa about 11% below its Oct. 2 close.
But Lula didn’t just beat Bolsonaro, he also beat prediction markets.
Polymarket gave Bolsonaro an 82% chance of winning the day before the vote, and Kalshi had him near 80% on Sunday morning. Both platforms are prediction markets, where a contract that pays $1 if a candidate wins trades at 80 cents when traders see an 80% chance.
Polling pointed to a coin flip rather than a favorite, with the latest Datafolha survey tied at 50% each among valid votes and CNT/MDA showing Bolsonaro ahead 50.5% to 49.5% in mid-October. Lula won 51.79% to 48.21%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro said on Sunday night that he does not recognize the result and will ask the courts to annul the election, after pledging in August to respect the outcome. He objected to Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting until 7 p.m. at the request of Lula’s campaign, which he said changed the rules midgame. His own campaign had separately asked for extra voting time in parts of three states.
“It is impossible to recognize the result of the elections in the context in which these things happened,” Bolsonaro said in Portuguese outside his campaign headquarters in Brasília. “We will use our legal team, we will ask for the annulment of these elections.”

In a stunning political comeback, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been elected president of Brazil, according to official results from Sunday’s runoff election, with more than 96% of the votes counted.
NPR reports that Lula secured more than 51% of the vote, defeating Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who received more than 48%.
The result marks a historic moment in Brazil’s democratic era. Since democracy was restored in 1989, no candidate who failed to win the first round of voting has gone on to win the presidency in the second round.
The victory also adds another chapter to Lula’s long political career, securing him a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, will be among the oldest sitting leaders in the Americas, alongside President Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, both 80.
In a speech to ecstatic supporters in São Paulo, Lula said the election was a “defeat of denialism. A defeat of lies.”
“I want to thank the Brazilian people for this generosity they have shown me for so long, to thank the youth who took to the streets to defend democracy, and the elders who went to vote,” Lula told the crowd.
Lula’s victory bucks a broader rightward shift across Latin America in recent years. In a pointed message to Trump, Lula declared that Brazil would not accept being “anyone’s backyard.”
Election day unfolded chaotically. Around midday, according to NPR, Lula’s campaign requested an extension of voting hours, arguing that some local governments had reduced bus services, making it harder for voters to reach polling stations.
Bolsonaro also sought an extension, citing heavy rain in some states.
Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours, to 7 p.m., but some polling stations had already deactivated their electronic voting machines and could not resume voting.
Speaking briefly to journalists outside his home in Brasilia, Bolsonaro called the result “inexplicable” and said he would seek to annul the vote. “I will not give up on my Brazil, and I hope you won’t give up either,” he said.
Bolsonaro, 45, had campaigned on closer ties with President Trump and pledged to pardon his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election defeat to Lula.
Brazilians showed little enthusiasm for street campaigning in the early months. But Bolsonaro’s first-round finish on Oct. 4 energized the contest, and in recent days supporters of both candidates have filled rallies and flooded social media in an effort to sway voters.
In the end, Lula’s message of continuity and a focus on social spending prevailed.
“I think people woke up about the risk of a Bolsonaro government after the first round, and the mobilization made a difference,” said Alessandra Miguel, a 35-year-old spa worker who voted for Lula in Rocinha, a favela in Rio de Janeiro.

Lula Secures Historic Fourth Presidential Term In Brazil After Dramatic Run-Off Comeback
Eighty-year-old left-wing leader and incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has secured re-election for a fourth term after defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a fiercely contested presidential run-off, completing one of the most remarkable political comebacks in Brazil’s democratic history.
With 99.77 per cent of ballots counted, Lula won 51.76 per cent of valid votes, while Bolsonaro received 48.24 per cent. The result marked a significant reversal from the first round of voting, when Bolsonaro had finished ahead, making Lula the first candidate since the restoration of direct presidential elections in 1989 to lose the initial round yet ultimately win the presidency in the decisive run-off.
The victory further cements Lula’s place in Brazilian political history. The Workers’ Party leader, who is now serving his fourth presidential term, extends his record as the second longest-serving holder of the office after Getúlio Vargas. Upon completing his latest term, Lula will have spent a total of 16 years in power, an unprecedented figure in Brazil’s democratic era.
The election campaign was dominated by concerns over the rising cost of living, public security and corruption. These issues shaped the political debate throughout the campaign and drove intense competition between the two candidates.
Lula, who first governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, entered the race facing significant political headwinds. Many voters expressed concern about inflation, household expenses and crime, creating a highly competitive environment for the incumbent president despite the advantages of office.
His challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, built his campaign around a tough-on-crime platform and promised measures aimed at reducing food prices and easing economic pressures on Brazilian families. The race remained extremely close throughout the campaign, with polls often indicating a virtual tie between the two contenders.
Both campaigns were also overshadowed by corruption controversies involving political allies and family members. Lula himself had previously spent more than a year in prison following corruption convictions that were later annulled by Brazil’s highest courts, paving the way for his political return and subsequent electoral victories.
Election day itself proved tense and highly charged. Voting hours were extended by two hours after last-minute appeals from both candidates to electoral authorities, reflecting the exceptional importance and competitiveness of the contest.
Lula’s victory carries implications well beyond Brazil’s borders. The result ensures that Latin America’s largest economy will continue pursuing a relatively independent foreign policy under Lula’s leadership. 
Throughout the campaign, he stressed Brazilian sovereignty while advocating stronger engagement with the Global South and maintaining close relations with China, even as tensions persisted with the administration of US President Donald Trump.
The scale of the comeback makes the result particularly noteworthy. Lula overturned a first-round deficit of nearly two percentage points to claim victory in the run-off, a feat never before achieved in modern Brazilian presidential elections. The result also demonstrated the continued strength of Lula’s support in key regions of the country, particularly in Brazil’s north-eastern states, which once again played a decisive role in the final outcome.
Born into a modest family and originally working as a factory labourer, Lula rose to prominence during the 1970s as a trade union leader. His activism helped transform him into one of Brazil’s most influential political figures.
He later co-founded the Workers’ Party and contested the presidency on three occasions before finally winning the office in 2002. His administration became known internationally for social welfare programmes and economic growth that lifted millions out of poverty. Lula secured a second consecutive term in 2006 before leaving office in 2010 with high approval ratings.
He was succeeded by his former cabinet minister, Dilma Rousseff, who went on to win the presidency in 2010 and was re-elected in 2014. Following years of political turbulence, corruption investigations and a period out of office, Lula returned to power and has now added a historic fourth presidential election victory to his political legacy.
Addressing supporters after the result became clear, Lula struck a conciliatory tone, emphasising national unity and reconciliation following one of the most polarised elections in recent Brazilian history. His latest victory not only extends his extraordinary political career but also opens a new chapter for Brazil as it confronts economic, social and geopolitical challenges in the years ahead.
